newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FEATURE - ABN AMRO earns global predator tag.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - ABN AMRO earns global predator tag.

text.p: Rarely a month goes by without ABN AMRO NV announcing a takeover or expansion of its operations spanning 70 countries around the globe, boosting its image as a hungry predator with deep pockets.
When the Netherlands' largest bank is not pursuing its growth path, it is being mentioned as a possible bidder for a bank in some part of the world.
"It's virtually every day that we are named in relation to a takeover all around the world," said bank spokesman Tanno Massar.
Its reputation is well deserved, having spent more than $4.0 billion on acquisitions since it was formed through a merger in 1990 of Algemene Bank Nederland and Amsterdam-Rotterdam Bank.
The pace of expansion has quickened in the last month with three purchases, including the largest to date, the $1.95 billion takeover of Standard Federal Bancorp.
Although it has stopped using the term "global bank" to describe its ambitions, ABN AMRO clearly wants to be a major player on the world stage of banking, analysts say.
They expect more acquisitions, particularly in the U.S. Midwestern states, where the banking industry is still highly fragmented and ripe for further rationalisation.
"They want to be where the growth is. That's what you see in their strategy. It's a bit of everything," said Heinie Hakker of BZW.
PLANS FOR GROWTH
The fifth largest bank in Europe and the fourteenth biggest in the world with $384 billion of assets at June 30, ABN AMRO's intention is to break into the world's top 10.
Most of the bigger banks in the world are Japanese, which are less internationally diversified, but the real rivals for ABN AMRO are seen as the major U.S. and European banks.
It plans to fill in gaps in its commercial, retail and investment banking operations around the world, with asset management often mentioned as an obvious area for growth.
Kempen and Co analyst Hans Pluijgers said ABN AMRO had been internationally diversified for decades but the pace of offshore expansion had accelerated in recent years.
"Since 1994 they have been looking more and more internationally. This year they have started to increase their expansion, particularly in Asia and Latin America," he said.
Already this year ABN AMRO has announced plans to inject $1.0 billion of capital into Asia by the year 2000 with the aim of doubling the contribution to group profits to 20 percent.
Its history in this fast-growing region dates back to 1826 when a predecessor bank opened a branch in Indonesia, then a Dutch colony.
Last month it bought Australia's Lloyds Bank NZA from a unit of Britain's Lloyds TSB Group Plc.

On a recent trip to South America, executive board chairman Jan Kalff said the bank planned to expand further in Brazil, the third biggest contributor to group profits after the Netherlands and the United States.
ABN AMRO has been operating in Brazil since 1917, providing trade finance to its corporate customers, and is very strong in consumer finance, particularly car loans.
INTEREST IN CORPORATE AND INVESTMENT BANKING

ING Barings analyst Daan Worm said ABN AMRO wanted to have strong positions in corporate and investment banking to exploit the synergies between them, such as underwriting equity issues for corporate borrowing clients.

The Dutch bank signalled its intention to bolster its previously weak position in investment banking when it bought London-based firm Hoare Govett in 1992 and moved to 60 percent of HG Asia last year.
The ambition was further underlined in May this year when ABN AMRO and the privately-owned Rothschild group merged their equity capital markets operations.
"They're a truly universal bank with a strong presence in the large corporate market. But that doesn't mean they will shy away from retail," Woorm said.

He said the U.S. Midwest states of Illinois, Michigan, Ohio and Indiana were becoming a second home market for ABN AMRO, which first entered the United States in 1979 after outgrowing the Dutch market.
The Standard Federal purchase entrenches its position as the largest foreign bank in the United States, where it mainly operates under the Lasalle name.
Analysts expect more small acquisitions in the region once Standard Federal is integrated into its U.S. operations.
Woorm said ABN AMRO saw the Midwest as attractive because plenty of small banks were available to buy, margins were high and cost savings could be made by integrating branches.
"They're looking everywhere for a position. They have a quite extended strategy. They're not a niche player," Worm added.
ABN AMRO continued to add to its operations in eastern Europe last month, buying 90 percent of Magyar Hitel Bank in Hungary for $89.23 million.
But the Dutch bank's desire to form a second home market in Europe has not been realised because of a lack of candidates which meet its requirement of immediately enhancing earnings.
"They have put aside the ambition. It's very expensive in France and Germany to buy big banks," Woorm said.

F Van Lanschot Bankiers analyst Jan-Paul van Bavel said ABN AMRO and Dutch financial services group ING Groep NV had transformed themselves in the eyes of the international community since they were formed through mergers.
He said they were regarded formerly as dull, but prudent provisioning had provided them with the financial muscle to grow organically and through acquisitions through the 1990s.
ING bought British merchant bank Barings in 1995 after it collapsed from derivatives trading losses.
"Both have the ability to be global players," van Bavel said.
